chapter_theme: Natrinai 121 to 140: secret loves of the hills kept on the clock of millet-guarding and pressed toward marriage, shore laments of gossip and lost play, heroes who argue their hearts out of journeys for wealth, and returns home through rain, with the friend speaking for, against and as the woman.

121.reading: The charioteer tells the hero, his work done and the king's leave given, not to fret: the town of the woman he loves lies in forest land where a young doe that nibbled the forked ears of millet rests beside her stag, and the plumed horses will cross the rain-cooled stream so that he may sleep tonight on the soft shoulders of the wife who is making ready the evening feast for guests.
121.nuance: The king's release is given in one clause and the rest of the poem is road and home: duty ends abruptly, and the charioteer measures the distance left by things the hero can see, the doe at rest, the stream bank falling behind, so that the wife's evening feast for guests becomes the poem's goal.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மறுத்தரும் தலைமகற்குத் தேர்ப்பாகன் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: millet fields, forest pasture and the deer pair of the mullai land, with a return home

comparisons.tenor: the wife's shoulders, rounded like bamboo

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the speaker is the charioteer (தேர்ப்பாகன்), not among the person codes

iraicchi.act: the doe, having fed on the millet ears, rests together with her stag
iraicchi.sense: the pair at rest after feeding promises the hero the same rest beside his wife tonight

122.reading: With the hero listening outside, the friend tells the girl that the red millet their brothers ploughed on the slope will soon be guarded, the jasmine by the hamlet has budded, the mother has turned a frowning face on her secret doings and asks whether the hill man really comes through the thunder-filled midnight, so the girl must herself decide how the flower garland can be made to fit, that is, how the man can be brought to marry.
122.nuance: Every detail is a clock for the man outside: the millet to be guarded, the jasmine in bud and the mother's question all say the meetings are nearly over, and the closing riddle of the garland leaves him to supply the word marriage.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகத்தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைப்பாளாய்த் தலைவன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: hill millet, the hamlet in the rocks and a night tryst nearing discovery

comparisons.tenor: the marriage that will bind the lovers openly

occasion.words: சிறைப்புறமாகத்தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைப்பாளாய்த் தலைவன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது

123.reading: With the hero outside, the friend asks the girl to speak: where flocks of fed herons crowd at dusk into nests among the curved fronds of the tall palmyra on the white sand, even their old games of the morning, weaving leaf skirts of fragrant cool lilies with the grove companions, running to the little striped play house, watching the crab at its wet hole under the kandal, have stopped, and the memory has become a great affliction.
123.nuance: The list of games is the real message to the listener: the girl who was a child of the grove in the morning is now unable to play, so the man who caused it must act; the only creatures with a settled home at nightfall are the herons.

colophon.thurai: தலைவன்சிறைப்புறத்தானாக தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைப்பாளாய்ச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, palmyra, mangrove and crab of the shore

iraicchi.act: the herons, having fed, come back together at dusk to crowd into their nests
iraicchi.sense: even the birds of the backwater return to a shared home at night, while the man still leaves the girl without one

124.reading: Told that the hero means to leave, the friend begs him not to go: she cannot bear a life of grief like the anril bird alone without its mate, and the season has come when the eengai buds, the athiral flowers on the sand dune, the deer's hooves sink in it, and bubbles slide over the cool pooled water like a vessel of molten silver.
124.nuance: The friend says யானும் ஆற்றேன், I myself cannot bear it, speaking in the first person for the woman; the season is offered as proof that a departure now would break the rule that men return before the rains.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவு உணர்த்தப்பட்ட தோழி தலைவற்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the friend tries to stop a departure; the seasonal things are of mullai and the shore

comparisons.tenor: the lonely life of the woman left behind
the bubbles sliding on the pooled rainwater

125.reading: The friend comforts the girl as the marriage is delayed: if we tell him we fear his coming at midnight, when the hungry male bear tears at the striped anthill, roaring so the snake trembles and breathing like a smith's bellows as it digs, and beg him to come to marry, then after a wedding on a good day on our hill he will not delay but take us to his own great hill country, where men in vengai garlands driving oxen on a floor as wide as open land wake the sleeping elephant as they stack the millet.
125.nuance: The bear at the anthill is the danger of his night road, and a reader may hear in it the man's own hungry coming (seeking at midnight, frightening those within); only one pair holds clearly, so it is left as scene, a near miss for ullurai. The poem's comfort lies in the contrast of nights: the fearful midnight here, the noisy harvest that wakes an elephant in his country.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு நீட்டிப்ப ஆற்றாளாய தலைவியைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது

thinai_evidence.note: bear, vengai and hill millet, with a night tryst and a wedding to come

comparisons.tenor: the bear breathing hard as it digs
the wide threshing floor

126.reading: The hero rebukes the heart that is set on wealth: across the ruined land where a dust-bathed bull elephant, hungry to find a man, blocks the path and, seeing no travellers, cools its rage on a palmyra, wealth won by crossing may give pleasure, but no wealth surpasses youth, and once youth has passed wealth cannot bring love, so go alone, heart, with your sickness for wealth that does not last, and may your business prosper.
126.nuance: The argument turns on a reversal of the usual order: wealth is called நில்லாப் பொருள், the thing that does not stay, and youth the true வளமை; the last line's blessing on the heart's business is ironic, since the man himself stays.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் வலித்த நெஞ்சினைத் தலைவன் நெருங்கிச் செலவு அழுங்கியது

thinai_evidence.note: the waste road and the elephant's rage, with a journey for wealth refused

127.reading: The friend turns away the bard: in this hamlet where the wet-backed stork that searched the backwater shivers in the flung spray, what if your man comes? The simple girl, whose brothers are the rough unlettered men who fill the rich fish-eating town, still takes up the doll she played with in the sand long ago and ponders it, and says 'let us go' only to the grove, not to the lord of the soft shore.
127.nuance: The refusal is made by calling the girl a child: the doll and the sand games say she is not yet a woman to be courted, and her fierce brothers say the courtship is dangerous. Refusing the bard's entry is usually marutham's oodal; here it is set wholly in shore things.

colophon.thurai: பாணற்குத் தோழி வாயில் மறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, stork and seaside grove

128.reading: The friend says the girl's body has paled like a lamp burning by day and her forehead's light is hidden like the moon the snake swallows, yet she has not told her who is like half of her own life, so let her stop weeping; and the girl answers that while she guarded the millet a man with a garland, an anklet and a chain came and coolly clasped her small back, and since then, with a heart full of that, this is the sickness she has.
128.nuance: Two similes of light put out by day and by eclipse make the friend's case before the girl speaks; the confession is all objects (garland, anklet, chain) and one touch, the clasp of the small back, which is the whole of the event.

colophon.thurai: தோழிக்குத் தலைவி அறத்தொடு நின்றதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the meeting in the millet field during its guarding

comparisons.tenor: the girl's paled body
her forehead whose light is hidden
the friend, as close as a half of the girl's life

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem itself sets the friend's question (lines 1 to 6) before the girl's confession; the colophon's other alternative has slipped into the text as line 12

129.reading: Hear a great joke, friend: the lover whose life changed if a single day passed without us says he will go, leaving us here with our thick hair, and says that we will live on in our house until he finishes his work and returns, and that while we hear alone, at midnight, the roar of thunder from the pouring clouds that makes the bright-hooded snake tremble.
129.nuance: The joke is the clash of his two sayings: the man who could not survive one day apart now proposes that we survive his whole absence; the closing midnight thunder is what 'we will live' will actually mean.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவு உணர்த்தப்பட்ட தோழி தலைமகளை முகம் புக்கது

thinai_evidence.note: the departure is announced; the night storm and snake belong to the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem's 'we' (நம், நாமே) speaks for both women

130.reading: Wasting in separation and unmoved by comfort, the woman says that for men of the old town of the chief, where the drum sounds at the centre and the morning's common work begins, nothing is sweeter than the life of their own work; however much they love, they do not think of us, and not once did he look at her yielding heart, loosened shoulders and faded lines and ask what this suffering one will do, so her pain, past the bounds of the sea-girt world, has no companion.
130.nuance: The complaint is general before it is personal: men find their own work sweetest; then it narrows to the one sentence he never said. The opening lines of chariot, drum and public work are hard to construe and the sense of 'red-water common work' is not secure.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை மெலிந்த தலைவி வன்புறை எதிரழிந்து சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: lament in separation, with no comfort accepted

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the friend who offered comfort; not named in the poem

131.reading: When the newly married hero praises the friend for keeping the girl from wasting, she answers: lord of the high sand shore, could we, whose sad hearts cannot even recall the games we played and the groves we rested in, have sulked at all? It was yours to forget, so that my shoulders, fair as Poraiyaru, fragrant with toddy, the town of Periyan of the fine chariot where the herons settle on the screwpine's shark-tooth leaves, grew loose.
131.nuance: She refuses the praise by refusing the credit: there was no sulking because there was not even strength to remember, and the wasting she prevented was his doing. She says என் நல் தோள், my shoulders, speaking as the girl.

colophon.thurai: மணமனையில் பிற்றை ஞான்று புக்க தோழியைத் தலைவன் வேறுபடாமை ஆற்றுவித்தாய் பெரியை காண் என்றாற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: screwpine, prawns and herons of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the thorned leaves of the screwpine
the girl's shoulders, spoken of as the friend's own

132.reading: The great town sleeps and no one is awake to help; the rain-laden cold wind, spilling from the shark-mouthed spouts onto the broad street, sprays through every chink of the strong doors so that the sharp-toothed dog trembles; the high flowered bed in the fine mansion has guards beside it, and above all the watchmen crying 'guard the gate' strike the long-tongued bell in double beats; is today, wretched as I am, the day I die?
132.nuance: The whole town is asleep but the house is not: wind, dog, guards and the watchmen's bell are a ring of wakefulness around one bed, so the sleeping town gives no help. The shark-mouthed spouts are carved work, not a creature of the shore, so the poem has no shore things.

colophon.thurai: காப்பு மிகுதிக்கண்ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைவிக்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a night meeting barred by the household's guard

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the closing lament (அளியேன்) is in the first person; the friend speaks it as the girl or the colophon's speaker is open to doubt

133.reading: The woman tells her comforting friend that her bangles keep slipping, her eyes have lost their sword-cut shape, pallor has spread over her forehead, and cruel-mouthed women spread talk about the dark girl with spotted skin and gem-bright hair; the loving friend's dear word that he will not cause us suffering is, to her sick heart, a small comfort, like the few drops a smith sprinkles from a dipped frond onto his hot furnace.
133.nuance: The simile measures the comfort exactly: a smith's sprinkle does not cool the furnace, it only checks it for a moment, and the closing சிறிதே, a little, is the poem's last word.

colophon.thurai: வரைவிடை வைத்துப்பிரிவு ஆற்றாளாய தலைவி வற்புறுத்தும் தோழிக்குச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: enduring the wait for marriage on the friend's word; no land is named

comparisons.tenor: the former shape of her eyes
her dark hair

comparisons.vehicle: கொல்லன் வெவ் உலைத் தெளித்த தோய் மடற் சில் நீர் போல
comparisons.tenor: the friend's comforting word to the sick heart

134.reading: The friend tells the girl, who feared she would be shut indoors, that this must be what is meant by sweet things coming upon sweet: the mother herself told her, 'mountain girl, go with your rattle to drive the red-beaked parrots from the millet on the hill where the lover set the sign of meeting', and the father, long may he live, said softly, 'won't you go, little one of bangles, let me kiss your sharp teeth', while she answered as if unwilling.
134.nuance: The comedy is that the parents send the girl to the very field where the lover waits, and the friend can only pretend reluctance; the 'sweet upon sweet' proverb is both the joy of the errand and the relief that the confinement feared has not come.

colophon.thurai: இற்செறிப்பார் என ஆற்றாளாய தலைவியை அ·து இலர் என்பது பட தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: millet guarding with rattles on the hill, the meeting place

135.reading: With the hero outside, the friend says their little seaside village, of sand-filled yards where palmyras with hanging leaves rise and the people of cool homes entertain arriving guests with gifts unstinted, was sweet indeed before the men of the chariot, whose white-plumed horses, worn from many dewy tracts, wheel and sink in the new sand of the roaring waves, began laughing with us.
135.nuance: The praise of a village that welcomes every guest is a pointed reproach: the man came as a guest and laughed with them but has not entered as a bridegroom, and since his visits the sweet village has become a place of talk.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு நீட்டிப்ப அலர்ஆம் எனக் கவன்ற தோழி சிறைப்புறமாகச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: palmyra village on the sand by the roaring sea

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; the girl is assumed

136.reading: With the hero outside, the girl tells her friend that when she wept for well-made bright bangles, her father, long may he live, as though he knew of the brief separation between them and the hill lord, did as a righteous physician does who, refusing the gravely sick what they crave, chooses a medicine and gives it: he fitted on her golden bangles that cannot slip off, a help that hides the blame her shoulders would tell.
136.nuance: She speaks for the man outside: the bangles that slip would announce her wasting, and the father's gold bangle, which cannot slip, hides it; the cure he chose treats the sign, not the sickness, which only the man can cure. The phrase நீப்ப நீங்காது வரின் வரை அமைந்து is hard to construe.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகத்தலைவி தோழிக்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord's secret love and a short parting

comparisons.tenor: the father who gives tight gold bangles instead of what she wept for

137.reading: The hero tells his heart that if it plans to leave the young woman of cool fragrant hanging hair and broad soft shoulders, it has achieved a rare thing indeed, being strong enough to go far through the hill-set forest of the long waterless stretch where the falls of the red rocks have ceased, where the crooked-trunked omai that a great tusker broke to ease the wasting hunger of his young cow-elephant becomes resting shade for those crossing the hard track.
137.nuance: The praise of the heart is ironic: the 'rare thing' it has achieved is hardness, and the road it would travel shows a beast that breaks a tree to feed its mate.

colophon.thurai: தலைவன் செலவு அழுங்கியது

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless road and a planned departure

comparisons.tenor: the woman's shoulders

iraicchi.act: the tusker breaks the omai tree to relieve the hunger of his young mate in the drought
iraicchi.sense: even the elephant in the waterless land feeds and stays by its mate, so the man who leaves his wife is harder than the beast

138.reading: With the hero outside, the friend tells the girl troubled by talk: the lord of the cool ford, where the white heron lays its eggs on the broken old cart floor left by bands of salt merchants who carry heaps of salt like hills up to the mountains to sell and abandon what fails them, once wove with us a garland of thick-stemmed neythal flowers; it was known only to our eyes then, but does the noisy old town, where festive women in fine girdles sway to the sweet beat of the waves, not know it today?
138.nuance: The heron nesting in the cart the wandering merchants abandoned could be read as the girl left by a passing man, but no second pair holds, so it stays scene. The contrast is between kinds of knowing: once only eyes knew, now the whole festive town does.

colophon.thurai: அலர் ஆயிற்று என ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகட்குத் தலைவன் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: salt, salt-merchants, neythal flowers and the shore ford

comparisons.tenor: the heaps of salt

139.reading: Back from his work and lying in the bedchamber, the hero blesses the great roaring cloud: may it spread over every peak of the hills set in many places as the world's linchpin and worshipped by many, for with drops like the plucked fine string of a lute tuned to the padumalai mode, humming like the clay-smeared face of the drum, it scattered mixed flowers and poured night rain on the slope town where he lay embraced with the dark woman of thick curled hair and enjoyed her sweetly.
139.nuance: A blessing is a thanksgiving: the cloud is praised as a helper (உதவியோயே) for a private night, and the poem's music images (lute string, drum) make the rain an accompaniment to the reunion.

colophon.thurai: தலைவன் வினைமுற்றி வந்து பள்ளி இடத்தானாக பெய்த மழையை வாழ்த்தியது

thinai_evidence.note: the rain at night after a return

comparisons.tenor: the hills that hold the world steady
the streaks and sound of the falling rain
the humming of the rain

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the rain cloud

140.reading: Refused, the hero tells his heart not to weary of following: the merciless girl who combs into five parts the sandal paste of the cool tree fed by the eastern rain clouds, sheds its dust when it dries on her cropped hair, and goes with her ball across the moonlit sand yard where her father's tall chariot runs, to her big-eyed companions' delight; whether she is kind or not, there is no other medicine to end the hard grief of the sickness he has.
140.nuance: The girl he cannot win is shown entirely at play, combing, scattering dust, chasing a ball, and the word பரிவிலாட்டி, the woman without pity, is fitted to a child who does not yet know she has been asked.

colophon.thurai: குறை மறுக்கப்பட்ட தலைவன் தன் நெஞ்சினை நெருங்கியது

thinai_evidence.note: a suitor refused in the courting stage

comparisons.tenor: the girl's favour, the only cure

links.note: Kural 1268 has the man wish that the king fight and win so that he may join his wife and hold the evening feast; in Natrinai 121 the charioteer reports that the king has let them go and drives him home to the wife preparing the evening feast for guests.
links.teaches: The couplet is a wish spoken while the war still holds him, the Natrinai poem the same wish granted and on the road, so together they show the full arc of the mullai return, and that the king's release and the evening guest-feast were the fixed terms of it.

links.note: In both a man returning from work passes a deer pair: in Akananuru 34 he himself sees the stag feed and guard his doe and urges the charioteer on; in Natrinai 121 the charioteer points to the doe resting with her stag to calm him.
links.teaches: The same deer pair works as a spur when the hero reads it and as a sedative when the charioteer offers it, so the mullai image carries a promise of home whose force depends on who in the chariot speaks.

links.note: In Kural 1155 the woman asks her friend, if she would guard her, to stop the man's departure; in Natrinai 124 the friend does exactly that, telling the man not to go and pointing to the season.
links.teaches: The Kural gives only the request, while the Natrinai shows the friend carrying it out, adding the rainy-season argument and the anril image, so the couplet's appeal is revealed as the opening move of a known scene in which the friend speaks for the woman to the man.

links.note: Naladiyar 16 says the fleeting pleasures of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling its garland, are not found among the wise; Natrinai 126 says no wealth surpasses youth and that love must be taken in youth because wealth cannot buy it later.
links.teaches: Both start from the shortness of youth and draw opposite duties from it: the Naladiyar to refuse youth's pleasure, the Natrinai hero to refuse wealth for its sake, so the same premise of impermanence served the akam poets as an argument for love and the didactic poets as one against it.

links.note: Both are poems in which the hero stops his heart from leaving; 126 argues that youth is worth more than wealth, 137 sets before the heart the tusker who breaks a tree to feed his mate in the drought.
links.teaches: The same thurai (செலவு அழுங்குதல்) is won once by reasoning and once by an animal example from the very road to be travelled, so the anthology shows two ways a hero could argue himself out of leaving: a calculation of value, or the shame of being harder than a beast.

links.note: Kural 1151 says: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 129 mocks as a great joke the man who says he will go and that we will live on at home until he returns.
links.teaches: Both turn the man's promise of return into a question of whether she will survive to see it, but the Natrinai supplies what the couplet leaves out, the midnight thunder she must hear alone, so the Kural's bitter one-liner has behind it a scene in which the waiting itself is the threat.

links.note: Kural 1168 has the sleepless woman say the night, which puts all creatures to sleep, has only her for company; Natrinai 132 begins with the great town asleep but fills the house with the cold wind, a trembling dog, guards by the bed and watchmen ringing the bell.
links.teaches: The couplet's solitude of the one waker is qualified by a poem in which others do wake, but only to keep her in, so the sleepless night of the guarded girl is not loneliness but confinement.

links.note: In Kural 1236 the woman, bangles slipping, is hurt when her friend calls the man cruel; in Natrinai 133, with the same slipping bangles, the friend says he will not cause them suffering, and the word gives the woman a little relief.
links.teaches: Held together they show the friend's two possible speeches and the woman's response to each, blame wounds her and defence of him comforts her, yet the Natrinai measures that comfort as a smith's sprinkle on a furnace, small and passing.

links.note: Kural 1157 says the bangles slipping past the wrist spread the news that the lord of the shore has left; in Natrinai 136 the father fits the girl with golden bangles that cannot slip, which hide the blame of her shoulders.
links.teaches: If, as the Kural says, slipping bangles are the body's gossip, the Natrinai shows that gossip could be silenced by a tight bangle, so the sign of separation was something a household could conceal, though only the lover could cure what it signified.

links.note: Kural 1146 says she saw him on only one day yet the gossip spread like the eclipse; Natrinai 138 says that their meeting at the ford was once known only to their eyes and asks whether the whole festive town does not know it today.
links.teaches: The Kural compresses into an eclipse the leap from one private sight to public talk that the Natrinai spreads over a remembered garland and a dancing town, and the Natrinai's overhearing hero shows the complaint was spoken to push him toward marriage.

links.note: Kural 211 asks what the world can give back to the rain, whose obligation seeks no return; in Natrinai 139 the hero blesses the rain cloud as his helper for the night rain that fell while he lay with his wife.
links.teaches: The Kural's rain serves the world and gets nothing back, while the Natrinai hero answers its private help with a blessing, so the poem shows the one return a person could make to the rain and turns the rain's public good into a favour done to two people.

links.note: In Kural 1102 the man says every disease has a cure other than itself, but this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes; in Natrinai 140 the refused man tells his heart there is no other medicine for the sickness he has.
links.teaches: The Kural states the paradox from the side of a man already united with her, the Natrinai from the side of a man refused, so the same claim that she alone is the cure is a joke in fulfilment and a sentence of endless pursuit in refusal.

links.note: In 122 the friend warns that the millet will be guarded and the mother frowns on the girl's secret doings; in 134 the mother herself sends the girl to drive parrots from the millet on the hill where the lover set his sign.
links.teaches: Millet-guarding is both the cover and the clock of the secret love: the same parental order that sends the girl to the field makes the meeting possible, and its ending, which 122 foresees, closes it, so the hill harvest sets the term within which the man must marry.

links.note: In Akananuru 91 the friend comforts the waiting woman with the elephant who in the drought shrinks together with his hungry mate; in Natrinai 137 the hero shames his own heart with the tusker who breaks an omai tree to feed his young mate.
links.teaches: The drought elephant that keeps faith with its mate is used by the friend to assure the woman that the man still loves her and by the man to accuse himself of leaving, so the image's single sense, even beasts do not desert their mates, could be turned to comfort or to reproach.

source_issues: 128: line 12 of the text (குறை நேர்ந்த தோழி தலைவி குறை நயப்பக் கூறியது) is a colophon thurai, not verse; it is the first alternative of the colophon, whose printed thurai ends ...நின்றதூஉம் ஆம். The poem is lines 1 to 11.

134: line 6 differs strongly from sangamtamil.com (ஏவினன் மன்னே நுந்தை, யாயும்); ours kept, and the sense of who spoke (mother or father) depends on it. The colophon thurai keeps the old encoding அ·து for அஃது.
124: colophon thinai நெய்தல்; the poem is a friend stopping a departure, with mullai things (ஈங்கை, அதிரல், நவ்வி) and the rainy season; I infer paalai, mixed.
129: colophon thinai குறிஞ்சி; the poem answers an announced departure, which I infer as paalai, with the night thunder and snake of the hills.

132: colophon thinai நெய்தல்; the poem is a guarded house at night in rain with no shore things, which I infer as kurinji. The closing lament is in the first person though the colophon makes the friend the speaker.
133: colophon thinai குறிஞ்சி; the poem names no land and turns on enduring the wait, which I infer as mullai.
130: lines 1 to 4 (the chariot drum and செந் நீர்ப் பொது வினை) are hard to construe.
136: line 7 (நீப்ப நீங்காது வரின் வரை அமைந்து) is hard to construe; the reading of the father as subject is mine.
